title: The Seven Chosen and Stephen Accused
summary: As the church grows, Greek-speaking Jewish believers complain that their widows are being overlooked in the daily food distribution. The apostles have the community choose seven men full of the Spirit and wisdom to oversee the work, and the word continues to spread, even among priests. One of the seven, Stephen, does great signs and argues powerfully in the synagogues, until opponents bring false charges and haul him before the council, where his face appears like the face of an angel.
story: Chapters 4 and 5 showed pressure from the authorities and a threat from dishonesty within. Chapter 6 adds a third kind of trouble: tension between two groups of believers along lines of language and culture. The church resolves it by sharing leadership, and the solution brings forward new leaders from the Greek-speaking group. Two of them, Stephen and Philip, will carry the story forward. Stephen's arrest leads to his great speech and death in chapter 7, and the persecution that follows will scatter the church into Judea and Samaria, where Philip will preach in chapter 8. A dispute about food distribution becomes the hinge by which the gospel moves beyond Jerusalem.
historical:
The setting is still Jerusalem in the early to mid 30s AD. The Grecian Jews (Hellenists) were Greek-speaking Jews, many of them born or raised in the Diaspora, the Jewish communities scattered across the Mediterranean world, who had settled in Jerusalem, sometimes in old age so as to die and be buried near the temple. That may explain why there were many widows among them. The Hebraic Jews were those whose main language was Aramaic (and who could read Hebrew), mostly natives of Judea and Galilee. Both groups were fully Jewish; the difference was language and culture.

The Synagogue of the Freedmen was probably a congregation of Jews who had been slaves, or were descendants of slaves, and had been freed; many Jews had been taken to Rome as captives after Pompey's conquest of Jerusalem in 63 BC. Luke lists men from Cyrene and Alexandria in North Africa and from Cilicia and Asia in Asia Minor. It is unclear whether one synagogue or several are meant. A Greek inscription found in Jerusalem in 1913 records a synagogue built by a priest named Theodotus for the reading of the law and with lodging for visitors from abroad; some scholars have connected it with a synagogue like the one named here, but that link is uncertain. Cilicia was the home province of Saul of Tarsus, who appears at Stephen's death.
cultural:
Widows in the ancient world, lacking a husband's income and often without sons nearby, were among the most vulnerable people in society. The Law of Moses repeatedly commands care for the widow, the orphan, and the foreigner (for example Deuteronomy 24:19-21). The Jerusalem church had taken on this responsibility with a daily distribution of food. Widows who had come from abroad, without extended family in the city, would depend on it heavily. A perceived bias in who was fed was a serious matter.

The laying on of hands was a gesture of blessing and commissioning drawn from Israel's Scriptures; Moses laid his hands on Joshua to commission him before the community (Numbers 27:18-23). All seven men chosen have Greek names, which suggests that the community chose leaders from the group that felt overlooked, a wise and generous response. Nicolas is described as a proselyte, a Gentile convert to Judaism, from Antioch, which hints at the Gentile mission to come.
literary: The chapter has two parts: the choosing of the seven (1-7), which ends with one of Luke's summary statements about the word of God spreading, and the beginning of Stephen's story (8-15), which continues into chapter 7. The second part echoes the trial of Jesus in many ways: false witnesses, a charge about destroying the temple, the council, and the elders and scribes stirred up. Luke may intend the reader to see Stephen following his Lord closely. The chapter uses the word full repeatedly for the qualities of the seven and of Stephen: full of the Spirit and wisdom, full of faith and the Holy Spirit, full of grace and power.

outline.t: The apostles propose seven to serve
Summary: the word spreads; many priests believe
False charges: against Moses and the temple

doctrines.note: The church faces its first internal conflict along cultural lines and handles it openly: the whole community is involved, qualified leaders are chosen from the group that felt neglected, and the apostles keep their focus on prayer and the word. Care for the needy is treated as serious ministry requiring people full of the Spirit and wisdom.

The qualifications for serving tables are spiritual: full of the Spirit and wisdom. Stephen's opponents cannot withstand the wisdom and the Spirit by which he speaks. In Acts the Spirit equips people not only for preaching but for practical service and for courageous witness.

Stephen is accused of speaking against the temple and the law and of saying that Jesus would change the customs of Moses. The charges are false as stated, but they touch a real question that the church will have to work out: how the coming of Jesus relates to the temple and the law. Stephen's speech in chapter 7 will address it.

words.note: Gongusmos, grumbling or murmuring. It is a sound word for low, discontented complaint. The Greek Old Testament uses the related verb for Israel grumbling in the wilderness (for example Exodus 16:7-8). Luke does not dismiss the complaint; the apostles take it seriously and fix the problem. But the word warns that grumbling can threaten a community's unity.

Diakonia, service or ministry. It appears for both the daily distribution of food (6:1) and the ministry of the word (6:4). Both are service. The related verb for waiting on tables (6:2) gives us the word deacon, and many Christians have seen the seven as the first deacons, though Luke never calls them that, and two of them are soon preaching and baptizing.

Hellenistes, a Hellenist or Grecian Jew: a Jew who spoke Greek and lived by Greek culture in many everyday ways. This was not unfaithfulness but a normal feature of Diaspora life. The Hellenist believers become a bridge for the gospel into the Greek-speaking world, and their leaders are the first to carry it outside Jerusalem.

christ: Stephen's story is told to echo the passion of Jesus. Like his Lord, he is full of grace and power, does wonders among the people, is accused by false witnesses of threatening the temple, and is brought before the council. The charge that Jesus would destroy this place recalls the charge at Jesus' own trial (Mark 14:58), and in John's Gospel Jesus had spoken of the temple of his body (John 2:19-21). The coming of Jesus does change the place of the temple and the way God's people relate to the law; that is the truth behind the distortion. The face like an angel's recalls Moses' shining face after meeting God (Exodus 34:29-35), a sign that the accused man, not his accusers, stands in God's presence.

hard.q: Were the seven the first deacons, and does this chapter set a pattern for church offices?
hard.a:
Luke never calls the seven deacons, though he uses the related noun and verb for their service. From the second century many Christian writers, and later many churches, have seen them as the first deacons, the office described in Philippians 1:1 and 1 Timothy 3:8-13. Others think they were a unique group appointed for a specific problem, more like assistants to the apostles or leaders of the Hellenist believers, and they note that Stephen and Philip are soon doing the work of evangelists rather than administrators.

Churches with different forms of government (episcopal, with bishops; presbyterian, with elders; and congregational, with the congregation governing) each find support for their practice here: the apostles propose and appoint, the elders are not yet mentioned, and the whole community chooses. What the passage does show clearly is a principle more than a structure: leaders delegate, the community has a voice, practical care is spiritual work, and those who serve must be of proven character. The details of church order are second-order questions on which faithful churches differ.

questions: The seven were chosen from the group that felt overlooked. What does that suggest about how churches should respond when some members feel neglected?
Serving tables required people full of the Spirit and wisdom. What practical work in your church deserves to be treated as spiritual ministry?
Stephen was falsely accused but kept his composure. How do you respond when you or your faith are misrepresented?
